text:
Epilogue


Samhain



The clapboard sign outside the Ferox Hall auditorium featured a very nice picture of Arthur Taliesin. He wore his new glasses with the black wire frames, and he had even persuaded Maggie to let him borrow his old tweed jacket. It looked good, not even a little bit threadbare.


She had taken many versions of this photo as the afternoon light streamed in through her apartment window. In many of the takes, he’d kept a serious expression with his signature furrowed brow, but in the one they’d sent off to Hawthorn’s marketing department, his lips were quirked in a half smile. Beneath his picture was the title of this afternoon’s lecture:



Alchemical Transformation for Technological Advancement Lecture Series: Metallic Conversions


Arthur Taliesin, Professor Emeritus


5:30 p.m. to 6:30 p.m.



Students were already leaving the hall, tugging their jackets close around their shoulders as the autumn wind met them. They talked excitedly about the lecture, about tonight’s festivities and their weekend plans. The parties they would attend, the costumes they’d wear, the person they hoped to find, masked, beneath the stars. Maggie smiled to herself as she listened to their chatter, shifting her legs as she sat on the steps, waiting.


Finally, after the stream of students and faculty died down, she heard one last person come through the doors of Ferox Hall and clear his throat. She twisted at her waist and grinned up at Arthur, who looked far too handsome in the glow of the lamplight that had finally flickered on as the sun set. He held out his hand and helped her up, gripping her waist and pulling her into him. She giggled as she wrapped her arms around his neck, and he leaned in to kiss her. She had never thought of herself as this light, airy woman, but he seemed to bring out the best in her. “Hello, Dr. Linden.”


“Good evening, Dr. Taliesin.” They untangled their limbs, reaching for each other’s hands as they walked down the steps of Ferox Hall.


“Do you have your costume ready?” she asked, and he smirked.


“It’s in my truck.”


Her lips curled into a wicked grin. “Let’s get it before we go upstairs.”


At Maggie’s apartment, he fiddled with his costume while she disappeared into her bedroom to find what she needed. When she emerged, he was wearing his Beltane mask and she was wearing hers. The magic had long worn off and the petals were dry and had curled at the edges, muted versions of the bright things they’d been on Beltane, but Maggie liked this mark of the passage of time. They were different people than they’d been that night; the masks should be different, too. “We have”—she glanced at the clock on her wall—“thirty minutes before we need to leave.”


“That’s plenty of time, I think,” he said, heat in his voice.


“To tell me about your day?” she said, getting closer, tugging him by the lapel of the tweed jacket until their bodies were flush together.


“My day was lovely. My twelfth graders were very excited about the candy I picked up at Glinda’s,” he said, nuzzling her neck. “I’m ready for my seminar with the Hawthorn first years. And today’s lecture attendees were very”—he pulled back to look at her so she would know exactly whom he was talking about—“enthusiastic. How was your day?”


He bent down to kiss her neck as she tried to talk, but words failed her as he distracted her with his tongue. “It went too slow,” she finally said. “I think my office is too quiet these days.”


He hummed against her skin. “I knew you’d miss me.” She did, and he knew it, but he was still Arthur, and she was still Maggie. She didn’t want to give him the satisfaction of admitting it.


“Oh, I almost forgot,” she said casually, “my translation was accepted to the Diadhan Review.” Arthur broke away just enough so she could see his wide smile. “So was my conference proposal.” She paused for dramatic effect and then added, “As part of the plenary session.”


“I knew it!” he shouted, gathering her into a spinning hug as her cheeks burned from the smile she couldn’t contain. Arthur might have known, but Maggie certainly hadn’t. He had listened to her fret over the submission materials and second-guess every word for weeks, cooking her dinner while she worked long into the night. She knew the proposal was good, but it was such a prestigious translation conference. In the moments she had wondered if it was a waste of time, Arthur had reassured her again and again.


“Thank you for believing in me,” she whispered.


“It’s easy to believe in you, Maggie.”


She walked backward as he kissed her, pulling him along, until the backs of her knees hit the couch. She sat and spread her legs, dragging him down with her until he was kneeling before her. The black tights she was wearing provided a thrilling challenge to what he truly wanted. Slowly, he pulled them down, one small inch at a time, anticipation coursing through Maggie like fire. Once he had them around her knees, he stopped, sitting up and kissing her again, keeping her legs pinned, deliciously, together.


“I love you,” Maggie said, and he sucked her bottom lip into his mouth, biting it gently.


He sat back on his knees between her legs, looking up at her like she was a vision. Like he still couldn’t believe it. “I will never get tired of hearing that,” he said reverently as his fingers slid up her stockinged calves toward the bare skin at her thighs.


She gasped as he tugged aside her underwear, the movement urgent with his want, and slipped two fingers inside her. Arthur had spent many weeks learning all the ways to drive her pleasure higher and higher, all the ways to make her squirm beneath his touch. He was a methodical researcher.


“We don’t have much time,” she reminded him.


“I’m not worried about that,” he said, crooking his finger inside her. “I know what you need.”


“If Dahlia were here, she’d make you put a dollar in the jar for that.”


The glass jam jar on the counter was nearly full of dollars and had a handmade label on the outside in Dahlia’s loopy handwriting—Arthur’s Full-of-Himself Fund.


“Well, I, for one, am very glad she isn’t,” he said, tugging her ear into his mouth and sucking.


“It’s good we have someone to keep you humble,” Maggie said, twisting her hips beneath his touch. She ran her fingers through Arthur’s hair as his tongue trailed a path down her cleavage.


When he pulled away, she gasped, but he kept his fingers working inside her, his other hand gripping her hip and pinning her down. His voice was low when he asked, “So you’re telling me this isn’t one of my many, many talents?”


“I didn’t say that,” she gasped.


“I can stop.”


“Don’t you dare.”


He rose up on his knees and leaned over her, the friction of his fingers curling inside her and his palm against her clit bringing her to the edge. When he brought his lips to her ear and whispered, “Come for me so we aren’t late,” she clenched around him and cried out. She kicked off her tights the rest of the way and gently pushed Arthur back on the floor, dragging his pants and underwear down until his erection was exposed. She slid him inside her slowly, and began to rock back and forth. He gasped, his hips bucking up into her.


“Make this quick,” she said, already working herself toward a second orgasm. His hands had returned to her hips, grinding her against him until she was coming again, and then it was only one, two quick thrusts before he groaned, filling her. They lay on the floor of Maggie’s apartment, spent, for just a moment.


“What if we stayed inside tonight instead?” Arthur asked, his mask on the floor next to him, lost as they’d chased their pleasure. He traced languid circles on Maggie’s hip.


“Absolutely not,” she said. “I’ve been waiting for this day for months. Months!”


He laughed. “Anything for you, love.” And he handed her the mask she’d lost, too.


They put their masks back on, cleaned up, adjusted their clothing, and started walking downtown to Rodrigo’s, which was decorated with large fluffy spiders and webs, stacked jack-o’-lanterns made of pumpkins and turnips glittering with heatless faefire, and a cool fog that swirled around the building on a loop. Inside, Rory and Dahlia were already at the bar with Jim, all decked out in costume.


“The mystery man,” Rodrigo said as they walked in, and Arthur gave him a shy smile. He held out a small yellow note card across the bar to Arthur.


“Rodrigo! That better not be what I think it is,” she cried, trying to reach for it, but Arthur held it over her head.


Rodrigo slid an old-fashioned across the bar in apology. “It absolutely is, sorry. This one’s on the house!” He left before she could scold him, returning to the end of the bar to offer Jim another drink.


“ ‘Calls himself TK…thirty-five’…” Arthur read. “You looked for me?”


Her cheeks turned rosy. “Well, Dahlia did.”


“I’ve been rooting for you all along,” Dahlia shouted across the bar.


He tucked the note in his pocket. It turned out, Arthur Taliesin was a sentimental fool. He’d probably pin it on the corkboard in his childhood bedroom at Barry’s house, right next to the spot where he’d kept the mask all this time. And she loved him for it.


He swept her into an easy kiss before pulling her into a hug, cradling her against him, his hand against the small of her back. She could hear his heartbeat beneath the fabric of his jacket and knew, with absolute certainty, that this was where she was supposed to be.


An excerpt from the epic Diadhan poem Branagh’s Aubade, translated by Dr. Magnolia Linden


[stanza 32]


Hand in hand, walking through eastern fields of gilded yarrow,


the near to autumn sun anoints your brow in shining crown.


Furrowed there in deep grooves like wounds, are tomorrow’s sorrows.


Bury my body, love, my bones. Hand in hand, lay me down.


I die neither brave nor willing as my blood salts the ground.


Your love burns bright, warm. A flickering fire, for me to find


beneath the yew, evergreen. Glory, glory for the crowned.


Bury my body, love, my bones. Hand in hand, intertwined.


My sword rusts, my flesh rots, but the yarrow grows on come morn,


the shade of the yew, remains, everlasting. Time forgets


but the soil remembers, each passing hour a root, a thorn.


Bury my body, love, my bones. Hand in hand, let me rest.

facts.fact: Samhain 海报：Ferox Hall 外 clapboard 招牌印他的照片（黑丝框新眼镜+借回的 tweed 一点不破旧）——Arthur Taliesin, Professor Emeritus 讲座。
学生闲谈回声：派对的戏服、星光下面具后希望找到的人——她微笑旁听（她已有答案）。
facts.anchor: the person they hoped to find, masked, beneath the stars

facts.fact: 旧面具重启：魔法早失效花瓣干卷——褪成 Beltane 的暗哑版；她喜欢时间流逝的痕迹：人不同了面具也该不同。
facts.anchor: muted versions of the bright things

facts.fact: 双喜临门：译文被 Diadhan Review 录用+会议提案入 plenary——他 I knew it!（她 certainly hadn't）；他做饭陪熬夜一遍遍 reassure。
facts.anchor: my translation was accepted to the Diadhan Review

facts.fact: 床笫方法论：黑丝袜 thrilling challenge；I will never get tired of hearing that（reverently）；他是 methodical researcher。
罚款罐：Arthur's Full-of-Himself Fund（Dahlia 的 loopy 手写）几乎塞满美元。
便签结案：Rodrigo 递出黄色便签 Calls himself TK…thirty-five——You looked for me?；她红脸 Well, Dahlia did；Dahlia 隔吧台喊我一直在为你加油。
sentimental fool：他把便签收进口袋准备钉上童年 corkboard、挂面具的位置旁——她爱他这一点。
闭环：她听着他外套下的心跳，全然笃定这就是她该在的地方。
facts.anchor: this was where she was supposed to be

facts.fact: 第 32 节压轴：Bury my body, love, my bones. Hand in hand, let me rest——yarrow 复生/紫杉长青/土壤记得（Dr. Magnolia Linden 译）。
